paras: The hanging of a Black man in Helton Township, Ashe County, was the killing of an unnamed Black man described as a "little negro dwarf" in northwestern North Carolina, reported in August 1881 as having taken place "not long since." He was hanged for allegedly stabbing a white girl, and the only report named the man who carried out the hanging as "a man by the name of Lynch."

According to a correspondent writing from the Virginia-North Carolina border, the man was "hung in Helton township" in Ashe County "for stabbing a white girl." The correspondent gave no date beyond "not long since," and did not name the victim or the girl or say how badly she was hurt. The hanging was attributed to a single named man, Lynch, and the item says nothing about whether anyone else took part, where the hanging took place, or whether a crowd was present.
The report mentions no arrest, trial or sentence before the hanging, and no report of an inquest or of any arrest afterward appears in the coverage.

The Western Sentinel of Winston, North Carolina, printed the item on August 25, 1881, as two sentences in a letter of border news signed "D. I." It ran between a jailbreak at Independence, Virginia, and a note on Davie and Alexander County travelers, alongside other items on violence near the state line, and carried no headline of its own. The correspondent stated the stabbing as fact and closed with the line "A man by the name of Lynch performed this Tristran hanging work," a phrasing that can be read as wordplay on lynching.
No second account of the hanging, in any paper, appears in the coverage, so the victim's name, the date and the circumstances rest on this one secondhand item.
